ui.howHeading: How the in-between frames are made
ui.how: We start from two real crystal structures of human hemoglobin: 4HHB without oxygen and 1HHO with oxygen. Every atom is matched by chain, residue and name. The two molecules are laid on top of each other so that the alpha 1 and beta 1 pair lines up, because the change between the states is described as one pair turning against the other. Then each atom slides in a straight line from its first spot to its second. Real molecules do not move in straight lines, and the oxygens arriving one by one is a drawing of the idea, not a measurement. Only the two ends are real.
ui.alt: A 3D model of human hemoglobin, about 7 nanometres across at its widest, made of four twisting protein chains: two alpha chains in pink and two beta chains in blue, each drawn as a tube that is thicker where the chain winds into a helix. Each chain cradles a flat heme ring with an orange iron atom in the middle. At the T end of the slider there is no oxygen and the irons sit slightly out of their rings. As the slider moves toward R, red oxygen molecules land on the irons one after another, each iron settles into its ring, and the alpha 2 and beta 2 pair turns against the alpha 1 and beta 1 pair, which is held still. Play swings the molecule back and forth between the two states like breathing.

T.t: No oxygen yet. The chains hold each other tightly, which makes the first oxygen hard to pick up.

mid.t: When an oxygen lands on an iron, it pulls a histidine on the far side of the heme. That small tug spreads through the chain and on to the other chains, so each new oxygen binds more easily.

R.t: All four irons hold an oxygen. One alpha and beta pair has turned against the other, and the molecule now holds oxygen more strongly.

hemeT.t: Without oxygen, the iron sits {v} angstroms out of the flat heme ring, pulled toward the histidine below it.

hemeMid.t: As oxygen binds on top, the iron slides into the ring and drags the histidine with it. This is the tug that starts the whole shape change.

hemeR.t: Now the oxygen molecule (red) sits on the iron, which is almost level with the ring: within {v} angstroms of it.

facts.t: Hemoglobin carries oxygen inside red blood cells. About 98.5 percent of the oxygen in your blood rides on it.
It has four chains, two alpha and two beta. Each chain holds a heme ring with one iron atom, and each iron can carry one oxygen molecule, so one hemoglobin carries up to four.
The oxygens do not all bind at once. The first is the hardest to add, and each one after it is easier, because the molecule changes shape as oxygen binds. This makes the oxygen curve S-shaped.
The shape without oxygen is called T, for tense: the chains hold each other back. The shape with oxygen is called R, for relaxed: it holds oxygen more strongly.
4HHB is human hemoglobin without oxygen in the T state. 1HHO is human hemoglobin with oxygen in the R state. Both were solved by X-ray crystallography.
Going from T to R, the two alpha-beta pairs turn about 15 degrees against each other.
Max Perutz proposed in 1970 how the four hemes talk to each other through the protein. Later crystal structures, including 1HHO, backed up his idea and the one by Baldwin and Chothia.
In sickle cell disease, one letter of the beta chain changes: glutamate 6 becomes valine. Without oxygen, these hemoglobins stick together into stiff fibres.
